Unison Energy Secures $120 Million Credit Facility From JPMorgan
By Amit Chowdhry
Oct 7, 2026
Unison Energy Secures $120 Million Credit Facility From JPMorgan
Unison Energy has closed a five-year, $120 million secured credit facility with JPMorgan Chase Bank to support the continued growth of its distributed energy and on-site power generation portfolio.
The facility also includes an additional $50 million accordion option, subject to credit approval, potentially providing Unison with additional capital as it develops and constructs new distributed energy projects.
Unison plans to use the financing both for its existing portfolio of energy assets and to fund development and construction of new projects.
The Greenwich, Connecticut-based company provides on-site power generation through an Energy-as-a-Service model for critical infrastructure facilities across North America.
Its customers include hospitals, data centers, food and beverage companies, industrial facilities, supply chain and logistics businesses, and hospitality organizations.
Unison designs, builds, owns and operates microgrids at customer locations. Its model is designed to reduce energy costs, improve resiliency during grid outages and lower carbon emissions without requiring customers to make upfront capital investments in the systems.
JPMorgan structured the new financing as a flexible warehouse-style facility.
The structure allows Unison to add and remove qualified projects from the borrowing base, subject to specified credit and operational requirements. That flexibility is intended to give the company a financing platform that can expand alongside its portfolio rather than requiring separate financing arrangements for each new project.
In addition to serving as lender, JPMorgan will act as Unison’s Hedging Provider and Depositary Bank for the transaction.
The financing follows a series of changes at Unison since Tiger Infrastructure Partners acquired the company in 2024.
Mariko Meier was appointed CEO in January 2026, while Al Dahya joined the company as CFO earlier this year.
Tiger Infrastructure has been working to expand Unison’s asset base, management team, and capital resources since making its investment.
The company has added new projects for multiple customers while investing in additional personnel to support its growth.
Unison and its investors see favorable conditions developing for distributed energy infrastructure as electricity demand rises and customers place greater emphasis on power reliability and resilience.
Those trends are particularly important for critical infrastructure and energy-intensive facilities where outages or constrained grid capacity can create significant operational risks.
The JPMorgan facility provides Unison with additional capacity to build new on-site generation projects as it seeks to expand its presence across those markets.
Support: Norton Rose Fulbright advised Unison on the financing. Milbank advised JPMorgan, while Black & Veatch served as Independent Engineer.
KEY QUOTES:
“Closing this financing with JPMorgan is a stepping stone for us, not an end point. Now the real work begins: putting this capital to work growing Unison and building new projects that power some of America’s most important places. We are excited to partner with JPMorgan who can bring the capital we need to support our long-term growth ambitions.”
Al Dahya, CFO of Unison Energy

Town Raises $108M at a $1B Valuation to Bring AI Assistants to Whole Teams
Now valued at more than $1B, Town extends its AI work assistant from individuals to whole teams
Tony Vincent
Jean-Denis Greze Published October 19, 2026
4 min
SAN FRANCISCO — October 19, 2026 — Town, the AI assistant built for teamwork, today announced a $108 million Series B. The round was co-led by Forerunner Ventures and Menlo Ventures. Existing investors a16z and First Round Capital also participated, along with Better Tomorrow Ventures, Precedent.vc, Scribble Ventures, Serena Ventures, Sparked Ventures, and notable angels, including Brendan Foody, Josh Silverman, Romain Huet, Scott Belsky, Steve Bartel, Taro Fukuyama, and Varun Anand. The round values the company at $1 billion.
Town is Built for Your Most Critical Work
AI personal assistants are beginning to handle the edges of everyday life: dinner reservations, flight changes, subscription cancellations. Those tasks lighten our mental load, but they sit on the margins of the day. Town is built for the center of it. Work fills eight or more hours of most people’s day, and it’s also how people make a living. So when context gets lost or decisions stall, the cost is highest at work.
At work, AI has already made each person far more productive on their own. But most work depends on other people: an updated model from finance, access to an app from an ops lead, input from the field sales team. The faster each person moves, the more they need from their teammates, and work slows to a crawl while they’re waiting for each other.
Today’s AI assistants can’t close that gap. A personal AI assistant knows its user but can’t work directly with the rest of the team. A team bot can see shared channels but can’t see anyone’s inbox or preferences, so it never really knows any one person. Neither can work well with people outside the company.
With Town, each person gets an AI assistant, called a Townie. A Townie connects to its person’s email, docs, calendar, and the core systems they work in. It learns their relationship context, projects, and voice, and takes work off their plate.
How Townies Work Together
Now, for the first time, those assistants can work directly with each other to move projects forward. They ask each other questions, connect the dots, and hand off work. Each Townie still works for its person. A Townie shares only what that person would share, asks permission when needed, and brings them the decisions that need their uniquely human eye. Townies can also work directly with customers, partners, and candidates outside the company over email and text.
Teams can also enable shared workflows. For example, when BizOps adds new fields to the competitor battle cards, it updates the team’s call-prep process once. From then on, every rep’s Townie preps calls with the new competitive analysis built in, updating materials to reflect the improved positioning.
“More people are trusting AI assistants with real tasks, and work is where they need the most help,” said Jean-Denis Greze, co-founder and CEO of Town. “Each Townie learns how its person works so it can take on their core work. Townies can ask each other questions and hand off work, so no one is stuck waiting. AI has made each of us faster on our own. Now, it can make teams faster together.”
